## 22. Swift packages design

One Swift package in `ios/sdk/`, `Package.swift` at its top (PD19), iOS 17 (PD11), products `CraftBridge` and `CraftBridgeEffects` (PD16). The engine start needs no processor check on iOS: every chip iOS 17 runs on (A12 and newer) has FP16. Apps reach it by local path during development and through `SwiftEffects` from the first release (D-24).

| Target | Change | What |
|---|---|---|
| `CraftBridgeFFIBinary` | NEW | `binaryTarget(path: "Frameworks/CraftBridgeFFIBinary.xcframework")`, named for the target and never for a crate, since the layer table says which library it holds (§15), built by `tools/build-xcframework.sh` and never committed; `SwiftEffects` carries `url:` and `checksum:` instead, the zip in its own release at the version's tag (`evidence/05-mobile-platforms.md` Finding 10, D-24) |
| `CraftBridgeFFI` | NEW, generated | UniFFI Swift for both crates, in `Sources/CraftBridgeFFI/Platform/Generated/`, where AGENTS §4's pointer rule holds (§20) |
| `CraftBridge` | NEW | the core's Swift API |
| `CraftBridgeEffects` | NEW | the EffectCraft API: hand-written fixed-shape calls plus `Generated/` (§21) |
| `CraftBridgeEffectsConformance` | NEW | the conformance corpus as Swift reads it, for the two test targets: the strict model of `corpus.toml`, how a scenario's folder is staged (its fixtures, the folder's path and a file's text in a request's parameters) and the listener that stops a call where its scenario says. A regular target in no product, so no app links it, since a test target can share no source with another and xcodebuild refuses one that depends on another; it takes the core's target alone and TOMLDecoder, so it makes no call of a plugin |
| `CraftBridgeEffectsTests` | NEW | Swift Testing: the conformance corpus on the simulator (QA-2) |
| `CraftBridgeEffectsPublicAPITests` | NEW | Swift Testing from outside the package's access: the two products' targets, the corpus's reader and `packageAccess: false`, so every call of the engine it makes is one another package can make, an app's or a binding's to another language; it holds the generic door to the typed calls over the corpus's requests, what `shutDown()` does, and that every type those calls take or answer has a name such a package can write |

**`CraftBridge` (core, hand-written):**
- `JSONValue` (`Codable`, literals), which crosses the boundary as JSON text, and `CraftError` (UniFFI's, with `LocalizedError` messages in the core's own words, read through `craft_error_message`, §14). `CraftError`, `Folders`, `ProgressListener`, `GpuChoice`, `PixelFormat`, `FrameBytes`, `Recovery` and `RecoveryNote` are UniFFI's own and are named from `CraftBridge` itself: the bindings module is no product, so the core's name is the one a package outside this one writes for each type a public call takes or answers, in a declaration of its own as well as where the compiler infers it. A name `CraftBridge` gives is one more a file can meet twice: a file that imports `CraftBridge` beside another module with a type of the same name writes that module's name before its type (`Accelerate.PixelFormat`, Accelerate having a protocol of that name), and a type of the app's own module keeps its plain name.
- `Folders.appDefault`: `Application Support/CraftBridge/{config,models,staged}` — the staged folder beside `config` and `models`, never under `Caches`, which iOS may empty while the app is not running and a saved project must still find the copies it names —, `Caches/CraftBridge`, the app's sandbox (`NSHomeDirectory()`) as the write root, so an export may go into `Documents`, which the Files app shows for an app that shares it, as well as `Library` or `tmp` — the start proves it can write there through the working folders' probes, since the top of the sandbox takes no new file on a device (§16) — and `Bundle.main` as the read-only root; `plugins` only through `Folders.appDefault.allowingPlugins(in: "PlugIns")`, a folder inside the bundle (PD13).
- `ClosureProgressListener`, the `ProgressListener` adapter from a closure of `done`, `total` and `secondsLeft`; `ExportJob` with `cancel()` and an `async` `result`; cancelling the `Task` that awaits the result sets the `CancelToken`.
- `Engine.attachMetalLayer(_ layer: CAMetalLayer)`, under `Platform/`: the one place a layer becomes `Unmanaged.passUnretained(layer).toOpaque()`, with its parameter typed `CAMetalLayer` since the Rust side trusts the class and takes a retain of its own (§20). `PreviewTarget` keeps the last layer an app previews into; the engine itself reports whether it holds a preview surface (`hasPreviewSurface()`, answered from the core, one definition both bindings share, §23), so `engine.preview(_:into:at:)` attaches the layer only when the engine is not previewing into this one, draws the frame of a composition at a time (`Duration`, turned into the engine's seconds in `previewRequest` as the nearest double to its whole nanoseconds, which is what Kotlin's own conversion gives, §23), and `engine.endPreview()` gives the surface up and makes the next preview attach afresh. The target's attaches and its ending take turns, each once the one asked for before it has ended, so two previews into two layers at once leave the engine on the layer the target remembers.
- `FrameBytes.pixelBuffer()` (under `Platform/`) → `CVPixelBuffer` (`kCVPixelFormatType_32BGRA`, IOSurface-backed, sRGB) and `FrameBytes.cgImage()` → `CGImage`, each from a frame asked for as `Bgra8Premultiplied`, whose bytes they hold as the core wrote them; any other format is refused.
- `BackgroundPolicy`: `.cpuWhenBackgrounded` (default: `suspendGpu` on entering the background, `resumeGpu` on return) or `.keepGpu` for apps running a `BGContinuedProcessingTask` with the GPU entitlement (§17, §25). `BackgroundController` applies it for the life of the engine (`EffectsEngine.start(folders:gpu:background:)`), and for whichever policy keeps every export out of suspension: each runs under a background task from its start to its end, and is cancelled when the system is about to stop the app. This holds whatever folders the engine was started in: a running export holds the pending-export journal's file lock, which iOS punishes in a suspended app when the config folder is in an App Group, and the GPU device it took at its start, whatever `suspendGpu` drops.

**`CraftBridgeEffects`:** `EffectsEngine.start(folders:gpu:background:)` and the fixed-shape calls, each a thin call into the engine method of §14's table that answers it: `exec`, `run`, `props`, `get`, `set`, `frame`, `export`, `replay`, `timings`, `previewRequest` and `mcp` are members of `EffectsEngine` itself, beside `recovery()`, which hands an app the generated `Engine.recovery()` it holds as it is, the whole report of what the start cleaned up after an export the system killed (§16, D-17), since the core's answer needs no shaping and an app reaches no `Engine` of its own (as `EffectsEngine.core.recovery()` does in Kotlin, §23), and `templates.open` and `templates.render` are hand-written extensions of the generated `templates` namespace's own type, so `engine.templates.open(…)` keeps that shape. `templates.open` answers a `TemplateInstance`, whose `set(_:_:)` and `set(_:media:)` run the commands `template.open`'s own values run — `essential.set` on the instance, in its own composition, after `file.import` for a media file — since §14's table has no method that sets a control of an instance already open. A public member written by hand never takes the base name of a public member the facade generates on the same type, neither a namespace's word on `EffectsEngine` nor a command's name on a namespace's type, since Swift would let a method with arguments stand beside either; the `swift_build` stage refuses one (AGENTS §9). `previewRequest(_:at:width:height:)` sends §14's `previewRequest` and answers a `PreviewRequest`: the `frame` request that fits the composition in the box (`request`, and `requestText`, the same request as the JSON text the engine wrote, which Kotlin answers byte for byte alike) and the composition's pixel size (`contentWidth`, `contentHeight`). These are the calls used in §5. The engine is ended by its `shutDown()`, the boundary's `shut_down` (§16, behaviour 4), which is what Kotlin's `shutDown` calls (§23), so it means the same on both platforms: an export still running is stopped as a cancel stops it, the preview's surface goes with the device, the call answers once the engine's thread has stopped, and every call made after it but `recovery()` throws `Internal` in the core's words, `engine is closed`.

**The generic door.** Under the typed calls three calls of `EffectsEngine` are public as well, as their like is in Kotlin, where `EffectsEngine.core` gives `request`, `requestWithProgress` and `frame(params, format)` (§23): `request(_:_:)`, one request of §14's table and its reply; `job(_:_:progress:)`, a method that reports progress, started as the `ExportJob` every such call is; and `frame(params:format:)`, a frame asked with the `frame` request's own keys. Each method is answered at one of the three alone, as the engine's own entry points divide §14's table: `request` refuses a method that reports progress, and `frame`, and a job of any other method is refused, each as `Unsupported` in words that name what that door answers. The typed calls that send a request, start a job or ask for a frame are each built on the one of the three that does it, so each of the three answers what the typed call over it answers for the same request. An app prefers the typed calls. The door is for a binding to another language, which carries every call as a method name with JSON parameters, so that a method the engine gains needs no native change. Each has a form in JSON text beside it, as Kotlin's has, for that binding: `requestJSON(_:params:)` answers the engine's reply as the text it wrote, `frameJSON(params:format:)` takes the keys as text and `jobJSON(_:params:progress:)` starts the job with them, whose answer `ExportJob.resultJSON` reads as the engine's text beside `result`. The `JSONValue` forms are built on the text ones, so there is one path to the engine, and the text passes the parameters through unparsed on the Swift side: text that is not JSON is the engine's to refuse, as `InvalidParams`, as Kotlin's door answers it, and a job's refusal is thrown by `resultJSON`. A `JSONValue` holds a number as a `Double` and an object in a dictionary, so a reply written back from one has a whole number the engine wrote as `2.0` as `2`, which Dart reads as an `int` where Android gives it a `double`, would lose a whole number's digits above 2^53, though the engine answers none today, and has the keys the engine writes sorted in an order that changes from one process to the next; the text keeps all of it, and builds no tree of values for a reply. A frame's layout and the frame, `PixelFormat` and `FrameBytes`, are among the types `CraftBridge` names (above), so such a package keeps a format or a frame in a declaration of its own. Which of the three a method takes is the engine's own table to say (§14): a binding sends each call through the one its caller chose by what it wants back, a reply, a job or a frame, and a method sent through another is refused before anything runs, in words that recite what that one answers, so no binding keeps a list of its own; an unknown method is refused the same way.

**Build.** `tools/build-xcframework.sh` runs `cargo xtask generate`, whose registered generator writes the Swift bindings into `Platform/Generated/` (§20), then `cargo xtask xcframework`, which builds the library the layer table gives the SDK (§15; `craftbridge-effects-ffi` while it has one app) with `--release` for `aarch64-apple-ios` (for the A12, the oldest chip iOS 17 runs on, whose half-precision instructions gemm-f16 needs: the CPU target `tools/env.sh` sets once for every device build, the gate's mobile stage and the device runner included) and `aarch64-apple-ios-sim` with `IPHONEOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET=17.0`, and joins the two static libraries, each with the crates' headers and one module map, with `xcodebuild -create-xcframework` into `ios/sdk/Frameworks/`. A static library carries no link flags, so each module map also links the system frameworks and libraries its library calls into, which an app's link then takes. Each fact is read from what owns it: the targets are the Apple targets `rust/rust-toolchain.toml` lists, the iOS version and the framework's folder are the package's manifest's, each library's file is the one Cargo reports building, and what it links is rustc's own answer for that library (`--print native-static-libs`), so a framework new platform code calls into is linked with no other edit. The framework is joined again only when a library Cargo rebuilt or a header changed, since a new one makes every Swift build that links it rebuild what imports it. The gate builds it before every stage whose ask needs the package to resolve — `guide_samples`, which asks `xcodebuild -showBuildSettings` what each sample's build compiles its Swift under, and so resolves the sample's local package, and the stages that build and test the package itself, `swift_build`, `swift_lint` and `swift_test` — with `--keep-bindings`, which leaves the committed Swift as it is so that the `generated` stage still finds a hand edit; the rules read the package through its manifest, which needs no native library.

**States.** Development (`ios/sdk/` by local path, the local XCFramework) · release (`SwiftEffects` by URL, the XCFramework downloaded from `SwiftEffects`'s own release and checksum-verified by SwiftPM).

**Tests.** Every target built in Debug and Release for the iOS device and the iOS Simulator in the gate; the corpus in Swift Testing on the iPhone simulator (QA-2) and on the acceptance iPhone (QA-3); and, in the same runs, the generic door and `shutDown()` from the test target that has no package access.
